modern:
Is there a church in this house? Are parents, children, friends and servants all members of it, or are some still unconverted? Let’s stop here and let the question go round the room: *Am I a member of the church in this house?* How father’s heart would leap for joy, and how mother’s eyes would fill with holy tears, if everyone from the oldest to the youngest were saved! Let’s pray for this great mercy until the Lord grants it to us.

Probably Philemon’s dearest wish had been to see his whole household saved, but at first it wasn’t granted to him in full. He had a wicked servant, Onesimus, who wronged him and ran away. His master’s prayers followed him, and at last, as God would have it, Onesimus was brought to hear Paul preach. His heart was touched, and he went back to Philemon, not only to be a faithful servant but a dearly loved brother, one more member of the church in Philemon’s house. Is an unconverted servant or child away from home this morning? Pray especially that when they come home, they’ll gladden every heart with good news of what grace has done! Is one here with us? Let him join in the same earnest prayer.

If there is a church like this in our house, let’s run it well, and let everyone act as in the sight of God. Let’s go about the ordinary business of life with careful holiness, hard work, kindness and integrity. More is expected of a church than of an ordinary household. In a home like that, family worship must be more devout and heartfelt, the love inside it must be warmer and unbroken, and its conduct toward the outside world must be holier and more like Christ. We don’t need to fear that being so few will strike us off the list of churches, for the Holy Spirit has written a family church here into the inspired book of remembrance. As a church, let’s now draw near to the great Head of the one universal Church, and ask him to give us grace to shine before people to the glory of his name.

modern: The doom was universal; neither rich nor poor escaped. The educated and the uneducated, the admired and the hated, the religious and the irreverent, the old and the young all sank in one common ruin. No doubt some had mocked the patriarch: where are their merry jokes now? Others had threatened him for his zeal, which they took for madness: where are their boasts and harsh words now? The critic who judged the old man’s work is drowned in the same sea that covers his sneering friends. Those who spoke patronizingly of the good man’s loyalty to his convictions, but didn’t share them, have sunk never to rise again; and the workers who were paid to help build the wonderful ark are all lost too. The flood swept them *all* away, without a single exception. In the same way, outside of Christ, final destruction is certain for every man of woman born. No rank, possessions or character will be enough to save a single soul who hasn’t believed in the Lord Jesus. My soul, look at this sweeping judgment and tremble at it.

How amazing the general indifference was! They were all eating and drinking, marrying and giving in marriage, until the awful morning dawned. There wasn’t one wise person on earth outside the ark. Folly fooled the whole human race: folly about saving themselves, the most foolish of all follies; folly in doubting the God who is perfectly true, the most spiteful foolishness of all. Strange, isn’t it, my soul? Everyone neglects their soul until grace gives them sense. Then they leave their madness behind and act like rational beings, but not until then.

*All* were safe in the ark, blessed be God; no ruin got in there. From the huge elephant down to the tiny mouse, all were safe. The timid hare was as secure as the brave lion, the helpless rock badger as safe as the hardworking ox. All are safe in Jesus. My soul, are you in him?

modern: It’s good for us that, amid all the ups and downs of life, there is One whom change can’t touch; One whose heart can never alter, and on whose brow the passing of time can leave no wrinkles. Everything else has changed, and everything is changing. The sun itself grows dim with age; the world is growing old; the folding up of the worn-out garment has begun; heaven and earth must soon pass away. They will perish; they will wear out like clothing. But there is One who alone is immortal, whose years have no end, and in whose person there is no change. The delight a sailor feels when, after being tossed about for many days, he steps onto solid ground again is the satisfaction a Christian feels when, amid all the changes of this troubled life, he rests the foot of his faith on this truth: “*I am the Lord, I change not*.”

The steadiness an anchor gives a ship when it has finally got a firm hold is like the steadiness the Christian’s hope gives him when it fastens on this glorious truth. With God “is no variableness, neither shadow of turning.” Whatever his attributes were long ago, they are now; his power, his wisdom, his justice and his truth are all unchanged. He has always been the refuge of his people, their stronghold in the day of trouble, and he is still their sure Helper. He is unchanged in his love. He has loved his people with “an everlasting love”; he loves them now as much as he ever did, and when everything on earth has melted in the last great fire, his love will still be as fresh as the dew of its youth. How precious it is to know for sure that he doesn’t change! The wheel of providence turns, but its axle is eternal love.

modern:
Prayer is the Christian’s never-failing resort in any situation, in every plight. When you can’t use your sword, you can turn to the weapon of all-prayer. Your gunpowder may be damp and your bowstring may have gone slack, but the weapon of all-prayer need never be out of order. Leviathan laughs at the javelin, but he trembles at prayer. Sword and spear need polishing, but prayer never rusts, and when we think it bluntest, it cuts best. Prayer is an open door that no one can shut. Devils may surround you on every side, but the way upward is always open, and as long as that road is clear, you won’t fall into the enemy’s hands. We can never be taken by blockade, by scaling ladder, by mine or by storm, as long as help from heaven can come down to us by Jacob’s ladder to relieve us in our time of need.

Prayer is never out of season: in summer and in winter alike, its goods are precious. Prayer gets an audience with heaven in the dead of night, in the middle of business, in the heat of noon, in the shadows of evening. Whatever your condition, whether poverty or sickness or obscurity or slander or doubt, your covenant God will welcome your prayer and answer it from his holy place.

Nor is prayer ever *futile*. True prayer is always true power. You may not always get what you ask for, but your real needs will always be met. When God doesn’t answer his children according to the letter, he answers according to the spirit. If you ask for coarse meal, will you be angry because he gives you the finest flour? If you ask for bodily health, should you complain if instead he makes your sickness work to heal the sicknesses of your soul? Isn’t it better to have the cross made holy than taken away? This evening, my soul, don’t forget to offer your prayer and request, for the Lord is ready to grant you your desires.

modern:
Prayers are noticed in heaven immediately. The moment Saul began to pray, the Lord heard him. Here is comfort for the soul that is distressed but praying. Often a poor brokenhearted person kneels but can only pour out his grief in sighs and tears; yet that groan has made all the harps of heaven thrill with music, and that tear has been caught by God and kept in heaven’s tear bottle. “Thou puttest my tears into thy bottle” implies that they are caught as they fall. The one praying, whose fears hold back his words, will be well understood by the Most High. He may only look up with misty eyes; but “prayer is the falling of a tear.” Tears are the diamonds of heaven; sighs are part of the music of Jehovah’s court, and are counted among “the sublimest strains that reach the majesty on high.” Don’t think that your prayer, however weak or trembling, will be ignored. Jacob’s ladder is tall, but our prayers will lean on the Angel of the covenant and so climb its starry rungs.

Our God not only *hears* prayer but *loves* to hear it. “He forgetteth not the cry of the humble.” True, he pays no attention to proud looks and lofty words; he cares nothing for the pomp and pageantry of kings; he doesn’t listen to the swell of military music; he takes no notice of human triumph and pride. But wherever there is a heart swollen with sorrow, or a lip quivering in agony, or a deep groan, or a sigh of repentance, the heart of Jehovah is open. He writes it down in the register of his memory. He puts our prayers, like rose petals, between the pages of his book of remembrance, and when the book is opened at last, a precious fragrance will rise from it.

modern:
One of the first qualifications for serving God with any success at all, for doing God’s work well and triumphantly, is a sense of our own weakness. When God’s warrior marches out to battle strong in his own strength, when he boasts, “I know I’ll win; my own right arm and my conquering sword will win me the victory,” defeat isn’t far off. God won’t go out with the man who marches in his own strength. Whoever counts on victory that way has miscounted, for “it is not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit, saith the Lord of hosts.” Those who go out to fight boasting of their prowess will come back with their bright banners dragged in the dust and their armor stained with disgrace. Those who serve God must serve him in his own way and in his strength, or he will never accept their service. Whatever people do without God’s strength, God can never own. He throws away the mere fruits of the earth; he will only harvest the grain whose seed was sown from heaven, watered by grace and ripened by the sun of God’s love.

God will empty out everything you have before he puts his own into you; he will first clear out your barns before he fills them with the finest of the wheat. The river of God is full of water, but not one drop of it flows from earthly springs. God will have no strength used in his battles except the strength he himself gives. Are you mourning over your own weakness? Take courage, for there must be an awareness of weakness before the Lord will give you victory. Your emptiness is only the preparation for your being filled, and your being cast down is only the making ready for your being lifted up.

modern:
No lips can tell the heart about the love of Christ until Jesus himself speaks within. All descriptions fall flat and tame unless the Holy Spirit fills them with life and power; until our Immanuel reveals himself inside, the soul doesn’t see him. If you wanted to see the sun, would you gather up all the ordinary lamps and try to see the great light of day by them? No, the wise person knows that the sun must reveal itself, and that mighty lamp can only be seen by its own blaze. It’s the same with Christ. “Blessed art thou, Simon Bar-jona:” he said to Peter, “for flesh and blood hath not revealed this unto thee.” Refine flesh and blood by any kind of education you like, raise the mind to the highest pitch of intellectual power, and still none of these can reveal Christ. The Spirit of God must come with power and overshadow a person with his wings, and then, in that mysterious holy of holies, the Lord Jesus must show himself to the eye that has been made holy, as he doesn’t to the half-blind children of men. Christ must be his own mirror.

The great mass of this bleary-eyed world can see nothing of Immanuel’s glories, which are beyond words. He stands before them with no form or beauty, a root out of dry ground, rejected by the shallow and despised by the proud. Only where the Spirit has touched the eye with eye salve, made the heart alive with God’s life and trained the soul to a heavenly taste, only there is he understood. “To you that believe he is precious”; to you he is the chief cornerstone, the Rock of your salvation, your all in all; but to others he is “a stone of stumbling and a rock of offence.” Happy are those to whom our Lord reveals himself, for his promise to them is that he will *make his home with them*. O Jesus, our Lord, our heart is open: come in, and never go out again. Show yourself to us now! Grant us a glimpse of your all-conquering beauty.

modern: This day stands out in English history for two great rescues God worked for us. On this day in 1605, the Roman Catholics’ plot to blow up our Houses of Parliament was discovered.
And second, today is the anniversary of King William III’s landing at Torbay in 1688, which crushed the hope of Roman Catholic rule and made religious liberty secure.

This day should be celebrated, not by the wild partying of boys, but by the songs of saints. Our Puritan forefathers kept it, with deep devotion, as a special time of thanksgiving. A record still survives of the sermons Matthew Henry preached on this day every year. Our Protestant feeling and our love of liberty should make us keep its anniversary with holy gratitude. Let our hearts and lips cry out, “We have heard with our ears, and our fathers have told us the wondrous things which thou didst in their day, and in the old time before them.” You have made this nation the home of the gospel, and when the enemy has risen against her, you have shielded her. Help us to offer repeated songs for repeated rescues. Give us more and more a hatred of Antichrist, and hurry on the day when she is wiped out entirely. Until then, and always, we believe the promise, “No weapon that is formed against thee shall prosper.” On this day, shouldn’t every lover of the gospel of Jesus feel moved to plead for false teaching to be overthrown and God’s truth to spread? Wouldn’t it be good to search our own hearts, and throw out any Roman Catholic junk of self-righteousness that may be hidden there?

modern: Our Lord wants all his people to be rich in high and happy thoughts about his blessed person. Jesus isn’t content for his brothers and sisters to think little of him; it is his pleasure that his bride should delight in his beauty. We aren’t to think of him as a bare necessity, like bread and water, but as a luxury, a rare and thrilling delight. To this end he has revealed himself as the “pearl of great price” in its matchless beauty, as the “bundle of myrrh” in its refreshing fragrance, as the “rose of Sharon” in its lasting perfume, and as the “lily” in its spotless purity.

To help you think highly of Christ, remember how highly he is valued beyond the skies, where things are measured by the right standard. Think how God values his Only Begotten, his gift to us that is beyond words. Consider what the angels think of him, as they count it their highest honor to veil their faces at his feet. Consider what the blood-washed think of him, as day and night they sing the praises he so well deserves. High thoughts of Christ will help us act in keeping with our relationship to him. The more loftily we see Christ enthroned, and the more humbly we bow at the foot of the throne, the better prepared we’ll be to play our part toward him. Our Lord Jesus wants us to think well of him so that we’ll submit cheerfully to his authority. High thoughts of him increase our love; love and high regard go together.

So, believer, think much about your Master’s excellences. Study him in his glory before time began, before he took your nature on himself! Think of the mighty love that drew him from his throne to die on the cross! Admire him as he conquers all the powers of hell! See him risen, crowned, glorified! Bow before him as the Wonderful, the Counselor, the mighty God, for only then will your love for him be what it should be.

modern:
When a believer has fallen into a low, sad state of mind, he often tries to lift himself out of it by punishing himself with dark and gloomy fears. That isn’t the way to rise from the dust, but to stay in it. You might as well chain the eagle’s wing to make it fly as doubt in order to grow in grace. It isn’t the law but the gospel that saves the seeking soul at first, and it isn’t legal slavery but gospel freedom that can restore the fainting believer afterward. Slavish fear doesn’t bring the backslider back to God, but the sweet wooing of love draws him to Jesus’ heart.

Are you thirsting for the living God this morning, and unhappy because you can’t find him to your heart’s delight? Have you lost the joy of your faith, and is this your prayer: “Restore unto me the joy of thy salvation”? Are you also aware that you are barren, like dry ground; that you aren’t producing the fruit for God that he has a right to expect from you; that you aren’t as useful in the church or in the world as your heart longs to be? Then here is exactly the promise you need: “I will pour water upon him that is thirsty.” You’ll receive the grace you need so badly, and you’ll have it to the furthest reach of your needs. Water refreshes the thirsty: you’ll be refreshed; your desires will be satisfied. Water wakes up sleeping plant life: your life will be woken by fresh grace. Water swells the buds and ripens the fruit: you’ll have fruit-bearing grace; you’ll be made fruitful in God’s ways. Whatever good quality there is in God’s grace, you’ll enjoy it to the full. You’ll receive all the riches of God’s grace in plenty; you’ll be drenched with it, so to speak. modern:
There is a strange power in the very word “blood”, and the sight of it always moves us. A kind heart can’t bear to see a sparrow bleed, and unless it’s hardened by habit, it turns away in horror at the slaughter of an animal. As for human blood, it’s a sacred thing: shedding it in anger is murder, and wasting it in war is a dreadful crime. Is this solemn feeling caused by the fact that the blood is the life, and pouring it out is the sign of death? We think so. When we rise to think about the blood of the Son of God, our awe grows even greater, and we shudder as we think of the guilt of sin and the terrible penalty the Sin-bearer endured. Blood, always precious, is priceless when it streams from Immanuel’s side.

The blood of Jesus seals the *covenant* of grace and makes it forever sure. Covenants in ancient times were made by sacrifice, and the everlasting covenant was ratified the same way. Oh, the joy of being saved on the sure foundation of God’s own commitments, which can never be dishonored! Salvation by the works of the law is a fragile, broken ship, sure to be wrecked; but the covenant ship fears no storms, for the blood makes the whole of it secure. The blood of Jesus made his *testament*, his will, valid. A will has no force unless the one who made it dies. In this light the soldier’s spear is a blessed help to faith, since it proved that our Lord was really dead. There can be no doubt about that, and we may boldly claim the legacies he has left for his people. Happy are those who see their right to heaven’s blessings secured for them by a dying Savior. But does this blood have nothing to say to us? Doesn’t it tell us to set ourselves apart for the one who redeemed us? Doesn’t it call us to new life, and urge us to give ourselves wholly to the Lord? Oh, that we might know and feel the power of the blood in us tonight!

modern:
No doubt part of the wonder packed into the word “*Behold*” is stirred up by the unbelieving complaint in the sentence before it. Zion said, “The Lord hath forsaken me, and my God hath forgotten me.” How amazed the mind of God seems to be at this wicked unbelief! What could be more astonishing than the groundless doubts and fears of God’s favored people? The Lord’s loving word of rebuke should make us blush. He cries, “How could I have forgotten you, when I have engraved you on the palms of my hands? How dare you doubt that I constantly remember you, when the reminder is cut into my very flesh?” Oh, unbelief, what a strange wonder you are! We don’t know which to wonder at more, the faithfulness of God or the unbelief of his people. He keeps his promise a thousand times, and yet the next trial makes us doubt him. He never fails; he is never a dry well; he is never like a setting sun, a passing meteor or a melting mist; and yet we are as constantly troubled with worries, harassed with suspicions and disturbed with fears as if our God were the mirage of the desert.

“Behold” *is a word meant to stir up wonder*. Here, indeed, we have something to marvel at. Heaven and earth may well be astonished that rebels should come so near to the heart of infinite love as to be written on the palms of his hands. “I have graven *thee*.” It doesn’t say, “Thy name.” The name is there, but that isn’t all: “I have graven *thee*.” See how full this is! I have engraved your person, your likeness, your situation, your circumstances, your sins, your temptations, your weaknesses, your needs, your works. I have engraved you, everything about you, all that concerns you; I have put the whole of you there. Will you ever say again that your God has forsaken you, when he has engraved you *on* his own palms?

modern:
To learn how to do your duty as a witness for Christ, look at his example. He is always witnessing: by the well of Samaria or in the temple at Jerusalem, by the lake of Gennesaret or on the mountainside. He witnesses night and day; his mighty prayers speak to God as clearly as his daily work. He witnesses in every situation: scribes and Pharisees can’t shut his mouth; even before Pilate he witnesses a good confession. He witnesses so clearly and distinctly that there’s no mistaking him.

Christian, make your life a clear testimony. Be like the brook where you can see every stone on the bottom, not like the muddy creek where you only see the surface. Be clear and transparent, so that your heart’s love for God and for people is visible to everyone. You don’t need to say, “I am true”: be true. Don’t boast of integrity; be upright. Then your testimony will be such that people can’t help seeing it. Never hold back your witness for fear of feeble man. Your lips have been warmed with a coal from the altar; let them speak the way lips touched by heaven should. “In the morning sow thy seed, and in the evening withhold not thine hand.” Don’t watch the clouds or check the wind. In season and out of season, witness for the Savior. And if it happens that for Christ’s sake and the gospel’s you must suffer in any form, don’t shrink back, but rejoice in the honor this gives you, that you are counted worthy to suffer with your Lord. Be glad of this too: your sufferings, losses and persecutions will make you a platform from which you’ll witness for Christ Jesus all the more vigorously and powerfully. Study your great Example, and be filled with his Spirit. Remember that you need much teaching, much upholding, much grace and much humility if your witnessing is to bring glory to your Master.

modern:
The life of faith is pictured as *receiving, an act that implies the very opposite of anything like merit*. It’s simply accepting a gift. As the earth drinks in the rain, as the sea receives the streams, as night accepts light from the stars, so we, giving nothing, share freely in the grace of God. By nature the saints aren’t wells or streams; they are only cisterns that the living water flows into, empty vessels into which God pours his salvation.

The idea of receiving implies *a sense of realization*, making the thing *real*. You can’t very well receive a shadow; what we receive is solid. So it is in the life of faith: Christ becomes real to us. While we are without faith, Jesus is just a name to us, a person who lived a long time ago, so long ago that his life is only history to us now! By an act of faith, Jesus becomes a real person in our heart’s awareness. But receiving also means *grasping or taking possession of*. What I receive becomes my own: I take to myself what is given. When I receive Jesus, he becomes my Savior, so much mine that neither life nor death will be able to rob me of him. All this is what it means to receive Christ: to take him as God’s free gift, to make him real in my heart and to claim him as mine.

Salvation may be described as the blind receiving sight, the deaf receiving hearing, the dead receiving life; but we haven’t only received these blessings, we have received *Christ Jesus* himself. It’s true that he gave us life from the dead. He gave us pardon for sin; he gave us righteousness credited to our account. These are all precious things, but we aren’t content with them; we have received *Christ himself*. The Son of God has been poured into us, and we have received him and made him our own. What a heartful Jesus must be, for heaven itself can’t contain him!

modern:
At Passover time Jerusalem was one great inn. Every householder had invited his own friends, but no one had invited the Savior, and he had no home of his own. It was by his own supernatural power that he found himself an upper room to keep the feast in. It’s the same even today: Jesus isn’t welcomed among the children of men, except where by his supernatural power and grace he makes the heart new. Every door is open wide enough to the prince of darkness, but Jesus must clear a way for himself or sleep in the streets. It was through the mysterious power our Lord used that the householder raised no question, but at once cheerfully and joyfully opened his guest room. Who he was and what he was, we don’t know, but he readily accepted the honor the Redeemer offered him.

In the same way, it is still found out who are the Lord’s chosen and who are not. When the gospel comes to some people, they fight against it and won’t have it; but where people receive it and welcome it, that is a sure sign that a secret work is going on in the soul, and that God has chosen them for eternal life. Are you willing, dear reader, to receive Christ? Then there’s nothing standing in the way: Christ will be your guest. His own power is at work in you, making you willing. What an honor to entertain the Son of God! The heaven of heavens can’t contain him, and yet he stoops to find a house in our hearts! We aren’t worthy that he should come under our roof, but what a privilege beyond words when he stoops to come in! For then he makes a feast and has us feast with him on royal delicacies. We sit at a banquet where the food is immortal and gives immortality to those who eat it. Blessed among the sons of Adam is the one who entertains the angels’ Lord.

modern:
If we have received Christ himself into our inmost hearts, our new life will show its close acquaintance with him by *a walk of faith in him*. Walking implies *action*. Our faith isn’t to be shut up in our prayer closet; we must put into practice what we believe. If a man walks in Christ, he acts as Christ would act; for since Christ is in him, his hope, his love, his joy, his life, he reflects the image of Jesus, and people say of him, “He is like his Master; he lives like Jesus Christ.” Walking means *progress*. “So walk ye in him”: go on from grace to grace; run forward until you reach the furthest degree of knowledge a person can reach about our Beloved. Walking implies *continuing*. There must be a constant abiding in Christ. How many Christians think they ought to come into Jesus’ company in the morning and evening, and may then give their hearts to the world all day! But this is poor living. We should always be with him, treading in his steps and doing his will.

Walking also implies *habit*. When we speak of a man’s walk and conversation, we mean his habits, the steady course of his life. Now, if we sometimes enjoy Christ and then forget him, sometimes call him ours and then lose our hold, that isn’t a habit; we aren’t *walking* in him. We must keep to him, cling to him, never let him go, but live and have our being in him. “As ye have received Christ Jesus the Lord, so walk ye in him”: keep going the same way you began. As at the first Christ Jesus was the object of your faith, the source of your life, the motive of your actions and the joy of your spirit, so let him be the same until life’s end; the same when you walk through the valley of the shadow of death and enter the joy and the rest that remain for the people of God. O Holy Spirit, enable us to obey this heavenly command.

modern:
Do you doubt, Christian, do you doubt whether God will keep his promise? Will the rock fortress be taken by storm? Will the storehouses of heaven run out? Do you think your heavenly Father, though he knows you need food and clothing, will still forget you? When not a sparrow falls to the ground without your Father, and the very hairs of your head are all numbered, will you distrust and doubt him? Perhaps your trouble will stay on you until you dare to trust your God, and then it will end. A great many people have been tried and badly troubled until at last, in sheer desperation, they were driven to put their faith in God; and the moment of their faith was the instant of their rescue. They have seen whether God would keep his promise or not.

Oh, I beg you, don’t doubt him any longer! Don’t please Satan, and don’t torment yourself by indulging those hard thoughts of God any more. Don’t think it a small matter to doubt Jehovah. Remember, it is a *sin*, and not a little sin either, but criminal in the highest degree. The angels never doubted him, nor did the devils: we alone, out of all the beings God has made, dishonor him by unbelief and tarnish his honor by distrust. Shame on us for this! Our God doesn’t deserve to be so meanly suspected. In our past life we have proved him true and faithful to his word; and with so many examples of his love and kindness as we have received, and are still receiving every day, from his hands, it is shameful and inexcusable that we let a doubt stay in our heart. From now on may we wage constant war against doubts of our God, enemies of our peace and of his honor; and with unstaggering faith may we believe that what he has promised he will also perform. “Lord, I believe, help thou mine unbelief.”

modern:
The word *refuge* may be translated “mansion,” or “abiding-place,” which gives the thought that *God is our dwelling, our home*. There is a fullness and sweetness in the picture, for our home is dear to our hearts, even if it is the humblest cottage or the barest attic; and far dearer is our blessed God, in whom we live and move and have our being. It’s at home that we *feel safe*: we shut the world out and live in quiet security. So when we are with our God we “fear no evil.” He is our shelter and retreat, our lasting refuge. At home *we take our rest*; it’s there we find rest after the tiredness and toil of the day. And so our hearts find rest in God when, worn out with life’s battle, we turn to him, and our soul is at ease.

At home, too, *we let our hearts loose*; we aren’t afraid of being misunderstood, or of our words being twisted. So when we are with God we can talk with him freely, opening up all our hidden desires; for if the “secret of the Lord is with them that fear him,” then the secrets of those who fear him ought to be, and must be, with their Lord. Home is also the place of our *truest and purest happiness*, and it is in God that our hearts find their deepest delight. We have a joy in him that far surpasses all other joy. *It’s also for home that we work and toil*. The thought of it gives us strength to carry the daily load and speeds our fingers to do the task; and in this sense too we may say that God is our home. Love for him strengthens us. We think of him in the person of his dear Son, and a glimpse of the Redeemer’s suffering face moves us to work for his cause. We feel that we must work, for we have brothers and sisters still to be saved, and we have our Father’s heart to gladden by bringing his wandering sons home; we long to fill the holy family we live among with holy joy. Happy are those who have the God of Jacob for their refuge like this!

modern:
No one will argue with this statement, for it would be unfitting for the servant to be raised above his Master. When our Lord was on earth, how was he treated? Were his claims acknowledged, his teaching followed, his perfections worshiped, by those he came to bless? No: “He was despised and rejected of men.” His place was outside the camp; carrying the cross was his work. Did the world give him comfort and rest? “Foxes have holes, and the birds of the air have nests; but the Son of man hath not where to lay his head.” This unwelcoming country gave him no shelter: it threw him out and crucified him. If you are a follower of Jesus and keep up a consistent, Christlike walk and way of life, you must expect the same treatment for the part of your spiritual life that shows on the outside, where people can see it. They will treat it as they treated the Savior: they will despise it.

Don’t dream that worldly people will admire you, or that the holier and more Christlike you are, the more peaceably people will act toward you. They didn’t value the polished gem; why would they value the jewel in the rough? “If they have called the Master of the house Beelzebub, how much more shall they call them of his household?” If we were more like Christ, his enemies would hate us more. It would be a sad dishonor for a child of God to be the world’s favorite. It’s a very bad sign to hear a wicked world clap its hands and shout “Well done” to a Christian. He may well start looking at his character and wonder whether he hasn’t been doing wrong, when the unrighteous give him their approval. Let’s be true to our Master, and have no friendship with a blind and wicked world that scorns and rejects him. Far be it from us to look for a crown of honor where our Lord found a crown of thorns.

modern:
God, the eternal God, is himself our support at all times, and especially when we are sinking in deep trouble. There are times when the Christian *sinks very low in humiliation*. Under a deep sense of his great sinfulness, he is so humbled before God that he hardly knows how to pray, because in his own sight he seems so worthless. Well, child of God, remember that when you are at your worst and lowest, still “underneath” you “are everlasting arms.” Sin may drag you ever so low, but Christ’s great atonement is still under it all. You may have gone down into the depths, but you can’t have fallen as low as “the uttermost”; and he saves to the uttermost.

Again, the Christian sometimes sinks very deep in *heavy trial from outside*. Every earthly prop is cut away. What then? Still underneath him are “the everlasting arms.” He can’t fall so deep into distress and affliction that the covenant grace of an ever-faithful God won’t still surround him. The Christian may be sinking under *trouble from within, through fierce conflict*, but even then he can’t be brought so low as to be beyond the reach of the “everlasting arms”: they are underneath him, and while he is held up like this, all Satan’s efforts to harm him come to nothing.

This assurance of support is a comfort to any *weary but earnest worker* in God’s service. It implies a promise of strength for each day, grace for each need and power for each duty. And further, *when death comes*, the promise will still hold good. When we stand in the middle of the Jordan, we’ll be able to say with David, “I will fear no evil, for thou art with me.” We’ll go down into the grave, but we’ll go no lower, for the eternal arms stop us from falling any further. All through life, and at its close, we’ll be held up by the “everlasting arms”: arms that never tire or lose their strength, for “the everlasting God fainteth not, neither is weary.”

modern:
Believer, if your inheritance is a humble one, you should be satisfied with your portion on earth, for you can be sure it is the best one *for you*. Wisdom that never errs ordained your lot and chose the safest and best situation for you. Suppose a large ship has to be brought up a river, and in one part of the stream there is a sandbank. If someone asked, “Why does the captain steer through the deep part of the channel and swing so far off a straight line?” he would answer, “Because I’d never get my ship into harbor at all if I didn’t keep to the deep channel.” In the same way, you might run aground and be shipwrecked if your divine Captain didn’t steer you into the depths of affliction, where waves of trouble follow one another in quick succession. Some plants die if they get too much sunshine. It may be that you are planted where you get only a little; you are put there by the loving Gardener, because only in that spot will you bear fruit to perfection.

Remember this: if any other situation had been better for you than the one you are in, divine love would have put you there. God has placed you in the most suitable circumstances, and if you had the choosing of your lot, you would soon cry, “Lord, choose my inheritance for me, for by my self-will I am pierced through with many sorrows.” Be content with what you have, since the Lord has arranged all things for your good. Take up your own daily cross; it is the load best suited to your shoulder, and it will do the most to make you perfect in every good word and work, to the glory of God. Down, busy self and proud impatience! It isn’t for you to choose, but for the Lord of love!

modern:
Untested faith may be true faith, but it’s sure to be little faith, and it’s likely to stay stunted as long as it has no trials. Faith never does so well as when everything is against her: storms are her trainers, and lightning flashes are her light. When the sea is calm, spread the sails as you like, the ship doesn’t move toward its harbor; on a sleeping ocean the keel sleeps too. Let the winds come howling out, and let the waters rise up; then, though the ship may rock, and waves wash over her deck, and her mast creak under the strain of the full, swelling sail, that is when she makes headway toward the harbor she longs for. No flowers wear so lovely a blue as those that grow at the foot of the frozen glacier; no stars gleam so brightly as those that shine in the polar sky; no water tastes so sweet as what springs up in the desert sand; and no faith is so precious as the faith that lives and triumphs in hard times.

Tested faith brings experience. You couldn’t have believed how weak you are if you hadn’t been made to go through the rivers; and you would never have known God’s strength if you hadn’t been held up in the floods. Faith grows more solid, more assured and more intense the more it is exercised by trouble. Faith is precious, and its testing is precious too.

But don’t let this discourage those who are young in the faith. You’ll have trials enough without looking for them: your full share will be measured out to you in due time. In the meantime, if you can’t yet claim the fruit of long experience, thank God for the grace you have. Praise him for the degree of holy confidence you have reached; live up to it, and you will still have more and more of God’s blessing, until your faith moves mountains and conquers impossibilities.

modern:
If anyone born of woman could have lived without prayer, it was our spotless, perfect Lord; and yet no one was ever so much in prayer as he! Such was his love for his Father that he loved to be much in communion with him; such was his love for his people that he longed to be much in intercession for them. *The fact* of Jesus’ outstanding prayerfulness is a lesson for us: he has given us an example so that we may follow in his steps. *The time* he chose was excellent. It was the hour of silence, when the crowd wouldn’t disturb him; the time of rest, when everyone but him had stopped working; and the season when sleep made people forget their troubles and stop coming to him for help. While others found rest in sleep, he refreshed himself with prayer. *The place* was well chosen too. He was alone, where no one would intrude and no one could watch, so he was free from Pharisee-like showing off and from the interruptions of the crowd. Those dark and silent hills were a fitting place of prayer for the Son of God. Heaven and earth, in the stillness of midnight, heard the groans and sighs of the mysterious Being in whom both worlds were joined.

*The length* of his pleading is remarkable. The long watches of the night weren’t too long; the cold wind didn’t chill his devotion; the grim darkness didn’t darken his faith, nor did loneliness hold back his persistence. We can’t watch with him one hour, but he watched for us whole nights. *The occasion* of this prayer is worth noticing. It came after his enemies had been enraged: prayer was his refuge and comfort. It came before he sent out the twelve apostles: prayer was the gateway of his undertaking, the herald of his new work. Shouldn’t we learn from Jesus to turn to special prayer when we are under a particular trial, or are planning fresh efforts for the Master’s glory? Lord Jesus, teach us to pray.

modern:
How did you begin to bear fruit? It was when you came to Jesus, threw yourselves on his great atonement and rested on his finished righteousness. Ah, what fruit you had then! Do you remember those early days? Then the vine really flourished, the tender grape appeared, the pomegranates budded and the beds of spices gave off their scent. Have you gone downhill since then? If you have, we urge you to remember that time of love, and repent, and do your first works. *Be busiest in the activities you have proved by experience bring you nearest to Christ*, because it’s from him that all your fruit comes. Any holy practice that brings you to him will help you bear fruit. The sun is no doubt a great worker at making fruit among the trees of the orchard, and Jesus is even more so among the trees of his garden of grace.

When have you been least fruitful? Hasn’t it been when you lived farthest from the Lord Jesus Christ, when you slacked off in prayer, when you drifted from the simplicity of your faith, when your graces took up your attention instead of your Lord, when you said, “My mountain standeth firm, I shall never be moved,” and forgot where your strength lives? Hasn’t it been *then* that your fruit stopped? Some of us have been taught by terrible humblings of heart before the Lord that we have nothing apart from Christ; and when we have seen the utter barrenness and deadness of all human power, we have cried in anguish, “From him all my fruit must be found, for no fruit can ever come from me.” Past experience teaches us that the more simply we depend on the grace of God in Christ and wait on the Holy Spirit, the more fruit we’ll bear for God. Oh, to trust Jesus for fruit as well as for life!

modern:
If *people* ought always to pray and not lose heart, Christians ought to all the more. Jesus has sent his church into the world on the same errand he came on himself, and this mission includes intercession. What if I say that the church is the world’s priest? Creation has no voice, but the church is to be its mouth. It is the church’s high privilege to pray and be accepted. The door of grace is always open to her requests, and they never come back empty-handed. The veil was torn *for her*; the blood was sprinkled on the altar *for her*; God constantly invites her to ask whatever she wants. Will she refuse the privilege angels might envy her? Isn’t she the bride of Christ? May she not go in to her King at any hour? Will she let this precious privilege go unused?

The church always has need of prayer. There are always some among her members who are going downhill or falling into open sin. There are lambs to pray for, that they may be carried in Christ’s arms; the strong, that they don’t grow overconfident; and the weak, that they don’t despair. If we kept prayer meetings going twenty-four hours a day, every day of the year, we might never lack a special subject for prayer. Are we ever without the sick and the poor, the troubled and the wavering? Are we ever without those who seek the conversion of relatives, the bringing back of backsliders or the salvation of the depraved? No: with congregations always gathering, with ministers always preaching, with millions of sinners lying dead in trespasses and sins, in a country on which the darkness of Roman Catholicism is certainly descending, in a world full of idols, cruelties and devilries, if the church doesn’t pray, how will she excuse her shameful neglect of her loving Lord’s commission? Let the church be constant in prayer; let every private believer cast his mite of prayer into the treasury.

modern: People like this thought they were safe because they were on both sides: they went along with the followers of Jehovah, and at the same time bowed down to Malcham. But double-dealing is detestable to God, and he hates hypocrisy with all his soul. The idol worshiper who openly gives himself to his false god has one sin fewer than the person who brings his polluted and hateful sacrifice to the temple of the Lord while his heart is with the world and its sins. To side with the hare and run with the hounds is a coward’s policy. In the ordinary business of daily life a double-minded man is despised, but in religion he is utterly loathsome. The penalty announced in this verse is terrible, but it is well deserved; for how could divine justice spare the sinner who knows what is right, approves it and claims to follow it, and all the while loves evil and lets it rule his heart?

My soul, search yourself this morning, and see whether you are guilty of double-dealing. You claim to be a follower of Jesus: do you truly love him? Is your heart right with God? Are you one of old Father Honest’s family, or a relative of Mr. By-ends? A name for being alive is worth little if I am really dead in trespasses and sins. To have one foot on the land of truth and the other on the sea of falsehood will mean a terrible fall and total ruin. Christ will be all or nothing. God fills the whole universe, so there is no room for another god; if, then, he reigns in my heart, there will be no space for another ruling power. Do I rest on Jesus crucified alone, and live for him alone? Is it my desire to? Is my heart set on doing so? If it is, blessed be the mighty grace that has led me to salvation; and if not, O Lord, pardon my sad offense, and unite my heart to fear your name.

modern: We don’t excuse Laban for his dishonesty, but we don’t hesitate to learn from the custom he gave as his excuse. Some things have to be taken in order, and if we want to win the second, we must first secure the first. The second may be lovelier in our eyes, but the rule of the heavenly country must stand: the elder must be married first. For instance, many people want the beautiful, lovely Rachel of joy and peace in believing, but they must first be married to the tender-eyed Leah of repentance. Everyone falls in love with happiness, and many would gladly serve twice seven years to enjoy it; but by the rule of the Lord’s kingdom, our soul must love the Leah of real holiness before the Rachel of true happiness can be won. Heaven doesn’t come first but second, and only by persevering to the end can we win a share in it. The cross must be carried before the crown can be worn. We must follow our Lord in his humiliation, or we’ll never rest with him in glory.

My soul, what do you say? Are you so vain as to hope to break through the rule of heaven? Do you hope for reward without work, or honor without toil? Put away that idle expectation, and be content to take the plain things for the sake of the sweet love of Jesus, which will repay you for everything. In that spirit, working and suffering, you’ll find bitter things grow sweet and hard things easy. Like Jacob, your years of service will seem to you only a few days, for the love you have for Jesus; and when the dear hour of the wedding feast comes, all your toils will be as though they had never been. An hour with Jesus will make up for ages of pain and work.

modern: How are they his? By his own sovereign *choice*. He chose them and set his love on them. He did this completely apart from any goodness in them at the time, or any goodness he foresaw in them. He had mercy on whom he would have mercy, and ordained a chosen company to eternal life; so they are his by his free choice, which nothing forced on him.

They are his not only by choice but by *purchase*. He has bought and paid for them to the last penny, so there can be no dispute about his title to them. The Lord’s portion has been fully redeemed, not with perishable things like silver and gold, but with the precious blood of the Lord Jesus Christ. There is no mortgage on his estate; no rival claimants can bring a lawsuit; the price was paid in open court, and the church is the Lord’s freehold forever. See the blood-mark on all the chosen, invisible to the human eye but known to Christ, for “the Lord knoweth them that are his.” He forgets none of those he has redeemed from among men; he counts the sheep he laid down his life for, and remembers well the church he gave himself for.

They are also his by *conquest*. What a battle he had with us before we would be won! How long he laid siege to our hearts! How often he sent us terms of surrender! But we barred our gates and fortified our walls against him. Don’t we remember that glorious hour when he took our hearts by storm? When he set his cross against the wall, climbed our ramparts and planted the blood-red flag of his all-powerful mercy on our strongholds? Yes, we are indeed the conquered captives of his all-powerful love. Chosen, bought and won like this, our divine Owner’s rights can never be taken from him. We rejoice that we never can be our own, and we long, day by day, to do *his* will and to show *his* glory.

modern:
It is our wisdom, as well as our need, to ask God constantly to strengthen what he has worked in us. Many Christians can blame their own neglect of this for the trials and troubles of spirit that come from unbelief. It’s true that Satan tries to flood the lovely garden of the heart and turn it into a wasteland; but it’s also true that many Christians open the floodgates themselves, and let in the dreadful flood through carelessness and failing to pray to their strong Helper. We often forget that the Author of our faith must also be its Preserver. The lamp that burned in the temple was never allowed to go out, but it had to be refilled every day with fresh oil; in the same way, our faith can only live by being fed with the oil of grace, and we can only get that from God himself. We’ll prove to be foolish virgins if we don’t secure the oil our lamps need. He who built the world holds it up, or it would fall in one tremendous crash; he who made us Christians must keep us going by his Spirit, or our ruin will be swift and final.

So let’s go to our Lord evening after evening for the grace and strength we need. We have a strong argument to plead, for it is *his own work of grace* we are asking him to strengthen: “*that which thou hast wrought for us*.” Do you think he will fail to protect and sustain that? Only let your faith take hold of his strength, and all the powers of darkness, led by the chief fiend of hell, can’t cast a cloud or a shadow over your joy and peace. Why faint when you may be strong? Why suffer defeat when you may conquer? Oh, take your wavering faith and drooping graces to him who can revive and refill them, and pray earnestly, “Strengthen, O God, that which thou hast wrought for us.”

modern: It isn’t “The Lord is *partly* my portion,” nor “The Lord is *in* my portion”; he himself makes up the whole of my soul’s inheritance. Inside that circle lies everything we have or want. The *Lord* is my portion. Not merely his grace, or his love, or his covenant, but Jehovah himself. He has chosen us for his portion, and we have chosen him for ours. It’s true that the Lord must first choose our inheritance for us, or we will never choose it for ourselves; but if we are really called according to the purpose of electing love, we can sing:

The Lord is our *all-sufficient* portion. God fills himself; and if God is all-sufficient in himself, he must be all-sufficient for us. It isn’t easy to satisfy human desires. When a man dreams he is satisfied, he soon wakes up to see that there is something still further on, and right away the horseleech in his heart cries, “Give, give.” But everything we could wish for is found in our divine portion, so that we ask, “Whom have I in heaven but thee? and there is none upon earth that I desire beside thee.” We may well “delight ourselves in the Lord,” who makes us drink from the river of his pleasures. Our faith stretches her wings and soars like an eagle into the heaven of divine love, her true home. “The lines have fallen to us in pleasant places; yea, we have a goodly heritage.” Let’s rejoice in the Lord always; let’s show the world that we are a happy and blessed people, and so lead them to exclaim, “We will go with you, for we have heard that God is with you.”

modern:
The more you know about Christ, the less you’ll be satisfied with shallow views of him; and the more deeply you study his dealings in the eternal covenant, his commitments on your behalf as the eternal Surety, and the fullness of his grace that shines in all his offices, the more truly you’ll see the King in his beauty. Spend much time looking like this. Long more and more to see Jesus. *Meditation and contemplation* are often like windows of agate and gates of carbuncle through which we see the Redeemer. Meditation puts the telescope to the eye, and lets us see Jesus in a better way than we could have seen him if we had lived in the days of his flesh. If only our lives were more taken up with heaven, and more absorbed in the person, the work and the beauty of our Lord who became flesh! More meditation, and the King’s beauty would flash on us with more splendor.

Dear friend, it’s very likely that we’ll have such a sight of our glorious King as we never had before *when we come to die*. Many saints, in dying, have looked up from the middle of the stormy waters and seen Jesus walking on the waves of the sea, and heard him say, “It is I, be not afraid.” Ah, yes! When the house of the body begins to shake and the clay falls away, we see Christ through the cracks, and the sunlight of heaven comes streaming in between the rafters. But if we want to see the “King in his beauty” face to face, *we must go to heaven* for the sight, or the King must come here in person. Oh, that he would come on the wings of the wind! He is our Husband, and we are widowed by his absence; he is our Brother, dear and fair, and we are lonely without him. Thick veils and clouds hang between our souls and their true life: when will the day break and the shadows flee away? Oh, long-awaited day, begin!

modern: “To whom be glory for ever.” This should be the Christian’s *one* desire. All other wishes must serve this one and feed into it. The Christian may wish for success in his business, but only so far as it may help him promote this: “To him be glory for ever.” He may want to gain more gifts and more graces, but only so that “To him may be glory for ever.” You aren’t acting as you should when you are moved by any motive other than a single eye to your Lord’s glory. As a Christian, you are “of God, and through God”; then live “to God.” Let nothing ever make your heart beat so powerfully as love for him. Let this ambition set your soul on fire; let it be the foundation of every undertaking you begin, and the motive that keeps you going whenever your zeal starts to cool. Make God your only aim. Depend on it, where self begins, sorrow begins; but if God is my highest delight and only aim,

Let your desire for God’s glory be a *growing* desire. You praised him in your youth; don’t be content with the kind of praise you gave him then. Has God made you prosper in business? Give him more, as he has given you more. Has God given you experience? Praise him with stronger faith than you had at first. Is your knowledge growing? Then sing more sweetly. Are you enjoying happier times than you once had? Have you been brought back from sickness, and has your sorrow been turned into peace and joy? Then give him more music; put more coals and more sweet frankincense into the censer of your praise. Honor him in the practical things of your life, putting the “Amen” to this doxology to your great and gracious Lord by your own personal service and growing holiness.

modern: Oppressors may get their way with poor and needy people as easily as they split logs, but they had better watch out, for it is dangerous work, and a splinter from a tree has often killed the woodcutter. Jesus is persecuted in every saint who is wronged, and he is mighty to avenge his dear ones. Success in trampling on the poor and needy is something to tremble at: if there is no danger for persecutors here, there will be great danger hereafter.

*Splitting wood is a common, everyday job, and yet it has its dangers*. In the same way, reader, there are dangers attached to your work and daily life, and it would be good for you to be aware of them. We don’t mean accidents by flood and field, or disease and sudden death, but dangers of a spiritual kind. Your work may be as humble as splitting logs, and yet the devil can tempt you in it. You may be a domestic servant, a farmhand or a craftsman, and you may be well shielded from temptations to the coarser vices, and yet some secret sin may do you harm. Those who stay at home and don’t mix with the rough world may still be endangered by their very seclusion. No one is safe who thinks he is. Pride may get into a poor man’s heart; greed may rule in a cottager’s breast; impurity may venture into the quietest home; and anger and envy and malice may creep into the most out-of-the-way country house. Even in speaking a few words to a servant we may sin; a small purchase at a shop may be the first link in a chain of temptations; merely looking out of a window may be the beginning of evil. O Lord, how exposed we are! How can we be kept safe? Keeping ourselves is too hard a job for us: only you yourself are able to keep us in such a world of evils. Spread your wings over us, and like little chicks we’ll huddle down under you and feel safe!

modern:
In this picture, which refers to the inner life of a believer, we plainly have the idea of *secrecy*. It is a spring *shut up*. Just as there were springs in the East with a building put up over them, so that no one could reach them except those who knew the secret entrance, so it is with the heart of a believer when it is renewed by grace: there is a mysterious life within that no human skill can touch. It’s a secret no one else knows; in fact, the very person who has it can’t tell it to his neighbor.

The text includes not only secrecy but *separation*. It isn’t the common spring that every passerby may drink from; it is kept and guarded apart from all others. It is a fountain bearing a special mark, a king’s royal seal, so that everyone can see it isn’t a common fountain, but one that has an owner and is set apart by itself. So it is with the spiritual life. God’s chosen were set apart in the eternal decree; they were set apart by God on the day of redemption; and they are set apart by having a life others don’t have. They can’t feel at home with the world or delight in its pleasures.

There is also the idea of *sacredness*. The spring shut up is kept for the use of one special person, and so is the Christian’s heart. It is a spring kept for Jesus. Every Christian should feel that he has God’s seal on him, and he should be able to say with Paul, “From henceforth let no man trouble me, for I bear in my body the marks of the Lord Jesus.” Another idea stands out: *security*. Oh, how sure and safe the inner life of the believer is! If all the powers of earth and hell joined together against it, that immortal life must still go on, for he who gave it pledged his own life to preserve it. And who “is he that shall harm you,” when God is your protector?

modern:
Christ is *everlasting*. We can sing of him with David, “Thy throne, O God, is for ever and ever.” Rejoice, believer, in Jesus Christ, the same yesterday, today and forever. Jesus always *was*. The Baby born in Bethlehem was united to the Word, who was in the beginning and by whom all things were made. The title Christ revealed himself by to John on Patmos was “Him which is, and which was, and which is to come.” If he weren’t God from everlasting, we couldn’t love him so devoutly; we couldn’t feel that he had any share in the eternal love that is the fountain of all covenant blessings. But since he was with the Father from all eternity, we trace the stream of divine love to him as much as to his Father and the blessed Spirit.

As our Lord always *was*, so he also *is* forevermore. Jesus isn’t dead: “He ever liveth to make intercession for us.” Turn to him in all your times of need, for he is still waiting to bless you. And further, Jesus our Lord always *will be*. If God spares your life to complete your full span of seventy years, you’ll find that his cleansing fountain is still open, and his precious blood hasn’t lost its power. You’ll find that the Priest who filled the healing fountain with his own blood is alive to cleanse you from all sin. When only your last battle is left to fight, you’ll find that the hand of your conquering Captain hasn’t grown weak: the living Savior will cheer the dying saint. When you enter heaven, you’ll find him there with the dew of his youth on him; and through eternity the Lord Jesus will still be the never-failing spring of joy and life and glory to his people. May you draw living water from this sacred well! Jesus always was, always is and always will be. He is eternal in all his attributes, in all his offices, in all his might, and in his willingness to bless, comfort, guard and crown his chosen people.

modern: Our days are few, and are far better spent doing good than arguing over matters that are of minor importance at best. The old schoolmen did a world of harm by their endless discussion of subjects of no practical importance, and our churches suffer a great deal from petty wars over obscure points and unimportant questions. After everything has been said that can be said, neither side is any the wiser, so the discussion does no more for knowledge than it does for love, and it’s foolish to sow in such a barren field. Questions on points where Scripture is silent, on mysteries that belong to God alone, on prophecies whose meaning is doubtful, and on mere ways of observing human ceremonies, are all foolish, and wise people avoid them. Our business is neither to ask nor to answer foolish questions, but to avoid them altogether; and if we follow the apostle’s command ([[Titus.3.8|Titus 3:8]]) to be careful to maintain good works, we’ll find ourselves far too busy with useful work to take much interest in unworthy, quarrelsome and needless disputes.

There are, however, some questions that are the opposite of foolish, which we must not avoid but face fairly and honestly, such as these: Do I believe in the Lord Jesus Christ? Am I renewed in the spirit of my mind? Am I walking not after the flesh but after the Spirit? Am I growing in grace? Does my way of life adorn the teaching of God my Savior? Am I looking for the coming of the Lord, and watching as a servant should who expects his master? What more can I do for Jesus? Questions like these urgently demand our attention; and if we’ve been at all given to nitpicking, let’s now turn our critical powers to a far more profitable use. Let’s be peacemakers, and try to lead others by both our teaching and our example to “avoid foolish questions.”

notes.note: “But avoid foolish questions, and genealogies, and contentions, and strivings about the law; for they are unprofitable and vain” ([[Titus.3.9|Titus 3:9]]).

modern:
In his deepest distress, Job cried out for the Lord. The longing of an afflicted child of God is to see his Father’s face again. His first prayer isn’t “Oh, if only I could be healed of the disease that’s festering all over my body!” or even “Oh, if only I could see my children brought back from the jaws of the grave, and my property restored from the hands of the robbers!” No, his first and uppermost cry is, “O that I knew where I might find *Him*, who is my God! that I might come even to his seat!” God’s children run home when the storm comes on. It is the heaven-born instinct of a soul touched by grace to seek shelter from every trouble under Jehovah’s wings. “He that hath made his refuge God” might serve as the title of a true believer. A hypocrite, when God afflicts him, resents the blow and, like a slave, would run away from the master who whipped him; but not so the true heir of heaven. He kisses the hand that struck him, and seeks shelter from the rod in the arms of the God who frowned on him.

Job’s longing for fellowship with God was made stronger by the failure of every other source of comfort. The patriarch turned away from his sorry friends and looked up to the throne of heaven, just as a traveler turns from his empty water skin and hurries off to the well. He says goodbye to earth-born hopes and cries, “O that I knew where I might find my God!” Nothing teaches us the preciousness of the Creator so well as learning the emptiness of everything else. Turning away in bitter scorn from earth’s hives, where we find no honey but plenty of sharp stings, we rejoice in him whose faithful word is sweeter than honey or the honeycomb. In every trouble we should first try to make God’s presence with us real to ourselves. Only let us enjoy his smile, and we can carry our daily cross with a willing heart for his dear sake.

modern:
Notice how *confidently* the prophet speaks. He doesn’t say, “I hope, I trust, I sometimes think, that God hath pleaded the causes of my soul”; he speaks of it as a fact beyond dispute: “Thou *hast* pleaded the causes of my soul.” With the help of the gracious Comforter, let’s shake off the doubts and fears that so spoil our peace and comfort. Let this be our prayer: that we may be done with the harsh, croaking voice of guesswork and suspicion, and be able to speak with the clear, musical voice of full assurance.

Notice how *gratefully* the prophet speaks, giving all the glory to God alone! You see, there isn’t a word about himself or his own pleading. He doesn’t credit his rescue in any measure to any man, much less to his own merit; it is “*thou*”: “O Lord, thou hast pleaded the causes of my soul; *thou* hast redeemed my life.” A Christian should always cultivate a grateful spirit, and especially after a rescue we should prepare a song for our God. Earth should be a temple filled with the songs of grateful saints, and every day should be a censer smoking with the sweet incense of thanksgiving.

How *joyful* Jeremiah seems as he records the Lord’s mercy! How triumphantly he lifts up the song! He has been in the low dungeon, and even now he is still the weeping prophet; and yet in the very book called “Lamentations”, clear as the song of Miriam when she struck her tambourine, shrill as the note of Deborah when she met Barak with shouts of victory, we hear the voice of Jeremiah rising to heaven: “Thou hast pleaded the causes of my soul; thou hast redeemed my life.” Children of God, seek a living experience of the Lord’s loving-kindness, and when you have it, speak of it confidently; sing gratefully; shout triumphantly.

modern:
Aware of how defenseless they are by nature, the rock badgers take to burrows in the rocks, and are safe from their enemies. My heart, be willing to learn a lesson from these feeble folk. You are as weak and as open to danger as the timid rock badger; be as wise in seeking a shelter. My best security is inside the fortress of an unchanging Jehovah, where his unalterable promises stand like giant walls of rock. It will be well with you, my heart, if you can always hide yourself behind the ramparts of his glorious attributes, every one of which guarantees safety for those who trust in him. Blessed be the name of the Lord, I have done so, and have found myself like David in the cave of Adullam, safe from my enemy’s cruelty. I don’t have to find out now how blessed the person is who trusts in the Lord, for long ago, when Satan and my sins chased me, I fled to the cleft of the rock, Christ Jesus, and in his pierced side I found a delightful resting place. My heart, run to him afresh tonight, whatever your present grief may be. Jesus feels for you; Jesus comforts you; Jesus will help you.

No king in his impregnable fortress is more secure than the rock badger in his rocky burrow. The master of ten thousand chariots isn’t one bit better protected than the little dweller in the cleft of the mountain. In Jesus the weak are strong and the defenseless are safe; they couldn’t be stronger if they were giants, or safer if they were in heaven. Faith gives people on earth the protection of the God of heaven. More than that they can’t need, and needn’t wish for. The rock badgers can’t build a castle, but they make use of what is already there. I can’t make myself a refuge, but Jesus has provided one, his Father has given it, his Spirit has revealed it, and look: again tonight I enter it, and am safe from every enemy.

modern:
Everything the believer has must come from Christ, but it comes only through the channel of the Spirit of grace. What’s more, just as all blessings flow to you through the Holy Spirit, so no good thing can come out of you, in holy thought, devout worship or gracious action, apart from the sanctifying work of the same Spirit. Even if the good seed is sown in you, it lies dormant unless he works in you to will and to do of his good pleasure. Do you want to speak for Jesus? How can you, unless the Holy Spirit touches your tongue? Do you want to pray? Sadly, what dull work it is unless the Spirit intercedes for you! Do you want to conquer sin? Would you be holy? Would you imitate your Master? Do you want to rise to the highest heights of spirituality? Do you want to be made like the angels of God, full of zeal and fervor for the Master’s cause? You can’t without the Spirit: “Without me ye can do nothing.” O branch of the vine, you can have no fruit without the sap! O child of God, you have no life within you apart from the life God gives you through his Spirit!

So let’s not grieve him or provoke him to anger by our sin. Let’s not quench him in even the faintest of his movements in our soul; let’s encourage every suggestion he makes, and be ready to obey every prompting. If the Holy Spirit is really so mighty, let’s attempt nothing without him. Let’s begin no project, carry on no undertaking and close no deal without begging his blessing. Let’s pay him the honor due to him by feeling our complete weakness apart from him, and then depending on him alone, with this as our prayer: “Open my heart and my whole being to your coming in, and hold me up with your free Spirit once I have received that Spirit in my inner being.”

modern: *He is to be envied*. It was good to be Martha and serve, but better to be Lazarus and enjoy fellowship. There are times for each, and each is fitting in its season, but none of the trees of the garden bear such clusters as the vine of fellowship. To sit with Jesus, to hear his words, to watch what he did and to receive his smiles was such a favor that it must have made Lazarus as happy as the angels. When it has been our happy lot to feast with our Beloved in his banqueting hall, we wouldn’t have given half a sigh for all the kingdoms of the world, even if that much breath could have bought them.

*He is to be imitated*. It would have been strange if Lazarus hadn’t been at the table where Jesus was, for he had been dead, and Jesus had raised him. For the risen man to be away when the Lord who gave him life was at his house would have been ungrateful indeed. We too were once dead, yes, and like Lazarus rotting in the grave of sin. Jesus raised us, and we live by his life. Can we be content to live at a distance from him? Do we fail to remember him at his table, where he graciously feasts with his brothers and sisters? Oh, this is cruel! We ought to repent, and do as *he* has told us, for his slightest wish should be law to us. To have lived without constant fellowship with the one of whom the Jews said, “Behold how he loved him,” would have been a disgrace to Lazarus. Is it excusable in us, whom Jesus has loved with an everlasting love? To have been cold toward the one who wept over his lifeless body would have shown great hardness of heart in Lazarus. What does it show in us, over whom the Savior has not only wept, but bled? Come, brothers and sisters who read this page, let’s return to our heavenly Bridegroom and ask for his Spirit, so that we may be on terms of closer friendship with him, and from now on sit at the table with him.

modern: Jacob, protesting to Laban, describes his own hard work like this: “This twenty years have I been with thee. That which was torn of beasts I brought not unto thee: I bare the loss of it; of my hand didst thou require it, whether stolen by day, or stolen by night. Thus I was; in the day the drought consumed me, and the frost by night; and my sleep departed from mine eyes.” Our Savior’s life here below was even more toilsome than that. He watched over all his sheep until he gave in his final account: “Of all those whom thou hast given me I have lost none.” His hair was wet with dew, and his locks with the drops of the night. Sleep left his eyes, for he spent whole nights in prayer, wrestling for his people. One night Peter must be pleaded for; soon another needs his tearful intercession. No shepherd sitting under the cold skies, looking up at the stars, could ever complain of the hardness of his work as Jesus Christ could have complained, if he had chosen to, of the severity of the service he gave to win his bride:

It’s sweet to think about the spiritual parallel in Laban’s demand that Jacob account for every sheep. If any were torn by wild animals, Jacob had to make good the loss; if any of them died, he had to stand as guarantor for the whole flock. Wasn’t the toil of Jesus for his church the toil of one who was bound as surety to bring every believer safely to the hand of the One who had put them in his care? Look at hardworking Jacob, and you see a picture of him of whom we read, “He shall feed his flock like a shepherd.”

modern:
The teaching of a risen Savior is extremely precious. The resurrection is the cornerstone of the whole building of Christianity. It is the keystone of the arch of our salvation. It would take a whole book to describe all the streams of living water that flow from this one sacred source, the resurrection of our dear Lord and Savior Jesus Christ. But *to know* that he has risen, and to have fellowship with him as the risen One, sharing his risen life, seeing him leave the tomb by leaving the tomb of worldliness ourselves: this is more precious still. The teaching is the basis of the experience; but as the flower is lovelier than the root, so the experience of fellowship with the risen Savior is lovelier than the teaching itself. I want you to *believe* that Christ rose from the dead, so that you sing of it and draw all the comfort you possibly can from this well-established, well-witnessed fact; but I beg you, don’t stop there.

Though you can’t see him with your eyes as the disciples did, I urge you to aim at seeing Christ Jesus with the eye of faith; and though, like Mary Magdalene, you may not “touch” him, you may still have the privilege of talking with him, and of knowing that he is risen, since you yourselves are risen in him to new life. To know a crucified Savior as having crucified all my sins is a high degree of knowledge; but to know a risen Savior as having justified me, and to realize that he has given me new life, making me a new creature through his own new life, is a noble kind of experience, and no one should rest satisfied with less. May you “know him, and the power of his resurrection.” Why should souls who have been made alive with Jesus wear the grave clothes of worldliness and unbelief? Rise, for the Lord is risen.

modern:
When we were united to Christ by faith, we were brought into such complete fellowship with him that we were made one with him, and his interests and ours became shared and identical. We have fellowship with Christ in his *love*. What he loves, we love. He loves the saints, and so do we. He loves sinners, and so do we. He loves the poor perishing human race, and longs to see earth’s deserts turned into the garden of the Lord, and so do we. We have fellowship with him in his *desires*. He desires the glory of God, and we work for the same. He desires that the saints may be with him where he is, and we want to be with him there too. He desires to drive out sin, and look, we fight under his banner. He desires that his Father’s name may be loved and adored by all his creatures, and we pray daily, “Let thy kingdom come. Thy will be done on earth, even as it is in heaven.”

We have fellowship with Christ in his *sufferings*. We aren’t nailed to the cross or put to a cruel death, but when he is insulted, we are insulted; and it is a very sweet thing to be blamed for his sake, to be despised for following the Master, to have the world against us. The disciple shouldn’t be above his Lord. In our measure we share with him in his *labors*, serving people by the word of truth and by deeds of love. Our food and drink, like his, is to do the will of him who sent us and to finish his work. We also have fellowship with Christ in his *joys*. We are happy in his happiness; we rejoice in his exaltation. Have you ever tasted that joy, believer? There is no purer or more thrilling delight to be known this side of heaven than having Christ’s joy fulfilled in us, so that our joy may be full. His *glory* awaits us to complete our fellowship, for his church will sit with him on his throne, as his dearly loved bride and queen.
